prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B049 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six of us ranked it first, but the case rests on the science. A gut hormone amplifies insulin secretion only when glucose is raised and also acts on appetite and gastric emptying. The active form of the peptide was identified. That knowledge was turned into drugs whose benefit is confirmed in large randomized trials for glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The principle is original, has been confirmed independently for decades and has visibly changed the field, which is the standard I apply: a specific discovery with a discernible change, not a career. I would keep the citation on the physiology and the active peptide and name incretin-based therapy as the consequence. That credits the discovery without making the Prize a reward for a drug programme, and it states the therapeutic payoff openly. Holst supplies the native peptide physiology in humans, Drucker the proglucagon-peptide biology and therapeutic rationale, and Mojsov the identification of the active truncated peptide, the entity on which every later analogue was built. I see no clean second part. Any second achievement would force a split of the three names that weakens the GLP-1 attribution.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and I cannot remove it from memory alone. The chair asks for primary-source evidence on Mojsov's priority and on Habener's role. I have no verified primary documents here and I rely on recollection. My recollection is that the Mojsov and Habener groups worked in parallel on proglucagon processing and on the truncated GLP-1(7-36) form, and that the dispute concerns who established the active form first and how credit should be shared, not whether the form was identified. That is a judgment call, and I should say so. A trio omitting Knudsen can be read as ignoring the medicine that reached millions of patients. A trio including her can be read as rewarding industrial optimization, and her seat would then lean on a priority question I regard as unsettled. For B014, the Eshhar gap is a real problem for a citation that names the receptor concept. It would have to be worded around costimulated CAR engineering and clinical translation, which is a narrower achievement.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps Knudsen in the third seat, arguing that acylation-based half-life extension was a conceptually new step and that her contribution is the least disputed in the historical record.
responses.response: I have reconsidered this and I still hold Mojsov, but not on the grounds that Knudsen's work is lesser. Your argument that acylation-for-albumin-binding is more than scale-up is fair, and I move closer to it than in round 1. The two readings differ on a purpose-of-the-prize question, not on a fact. A citation on discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form is the more defensible line, because the analogues presuppose that form. Your point that an undisputed contributor carries less risk than a disputed one is the strongest argument on your side. My test is whether the Mojsov priority claim can be defended in the citation as a matter of degree. I believe it can, since nobody disputes that she identified the active peptide, and I would not call it settled. If the committee decides the citation must explicitly cover the long-acting drugs, then Knudsen should replace Mojsov, because a four-name arc cannot be fitted into three. Your statement that you would not block the Mojsov trio makes it easier to find a majority without papering over the disagreement.

responses.point: Svenningsson says the citation should centre on the hormone's biology and active form so that it rewards neither the pharmaceutical programme nor the chemistry alone, and that he could accept Knudsen if the committee openly chooses to recognise development.
responses.response: I agree with this framing and have adopted its wording. My round-1 citation tied the physiology to the therapy, and I now state the active form explicitly, which keeps Mojsov's contribution in the citation. I also share your admission that the priority history is recollection. The chair asked whether naming the therapy would change who is credited. I think it should not change the trio by itself. The citation can say that the physiology made incretin-based therapy possible without claiming that the Prize covers the drug design. Only an explicit statement that it recognises the development of long-acting analogues would shift the seat to Knudsen. You also say a second part is hard within the three-name cap. I agree and I do not propose one.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks for a consistent discovery-versus-development standard across GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T, and argues that CAR-T's autoimmune extension strengthens its case.
responses.response: I will state the standard I would apply to all three. The Prize recognises the discovery that opened a field, here a physiological principle or a mechanistic insight. It can recognise a clinical demonstration when that demonstration is itself the conceptual step, but not when it is optimisation of an existing mechanism. By that test GLP-1 passes on the physiology and active peptide. Imatinib is closer to a development prize, since the target and the mechanism were defined by others, although the proof of concept in CML was transformative. CAR-T falls in between, because costimulatory design and clinical proof are real conceptual steps, but the receptor concept is Eshhar's and sits outside the credited names. I accept your point that the autoimmune extension strengthens B014, and it is why I keep B014 as my first alternative. It does not remove my view that it is less settled than GLP-1, given the remaining toxicity and solid-tumour limits. I still rank B049 ahead of it.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers a single-part B049 prize and treats CAR-T as the strongest alternative rather than a co-equal second part. He also says the blunt call on GLP-1 deserves more scrutiny, not less.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The scrutiny worry is a fair one, and my response is to test the configuration against its weakest seat rather than to rely on the unanimous first place. The weakest seat is the third one, and I have laid out above on what condition I would change it. I also see no scientific reason to pair B014 with B049. A June and Sadelain pair takes two of the three names, and the GLP-1 trio would then need to drop to one. That cannot be done without injustice to Holst or Drucker. If the committee did want two parts, the cleaner path would be to treat CAR-T as its own prize in a later year, once the Eshhar question and the toxicity profile are better understood.

responses.point: El-Manira says optogenetics has no stable three-person configuration and that he would support it only if the channelrhodopsin discovery is credited as its own achievement. He also notes that long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 therapy are still accumulating.
responses.response: On optogenetics I agree that the attribution is not stable, and I am keeping it only as a second alternative. My own trio of Bamberg, Nagel and Hegemann credits the molecular discovery of channelrhodopsin. It leaves out the neuronal demonstration, so I accept your objection that it is a molecular-discovery prize and not a prize for the tool as used. A configuration that omits Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenboeck will be attacked, and I have no way to avoid that within three names. On long-term safety, I take the point that durability is still accumulating. I do not think that weakens the discovery case, which rests on the physiology, but it argues for a citation that does not overstate the clinical claims.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide, relative to Habener's group, can be defended to the standard a citation requires. My view rests on recollection of the history, not on primary documents I have verified.
Whether the committee, in its final decision, wants the citation to cover the long-acting analogues, because that would move the third seat from Mojsov to Knudsen.
Whether the discovery-versus-development standard I stated for GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T would be accepted by the other members or whether it hides a real difference in how we weigh clinical proof.
Whether a stable three-name optogenetics configuration exists. I do not think one does on the supplied credit.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. My documented collaboration with Ronald Evans and Johan Ericson, and past co-authorship with Svenningsson and El-Manira, concern people and work unrelated to the shortlisted candidates. None has changed since round 1.
